nameStory: Japanese kerria gets its name from its homeland of Japan (though it's actually native to both China and Japan). The genus name 'Kerria' honors William Kerr, a Scottish gardener who collected plants in China in the early 1800s and helped introduce many Asian species to Western gardens.
description: Japanese kerria is a cheerful deciduous shrub that brightens up shady spots with its golden-yellow flowers. Growing 3-6 feet tall and wide, it has an arching, graceful habit with bright green stems that stay colorful even in winter. Despite being in the rose family, it doesn't have thorns like true roses, making it much friendlier to brush against. The shrub spreads by underground runners, often forming colonies over time.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers with 5 rounded petals that look like buttercups, blooming in spring. Each flower is about 1-2 inches across and appears singly along the branches, never in clusters.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Gracefully arching branches that fountain outward from the base, creating a mounded shape. The shrub spreads by underground runners and often forms small colonies.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval, pointed leaves with prominent parallel veins and toothed edges that feel papery-thin. They're bright green in summer and turn yellow in fall before dropping.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are bright green year-round, while older bark becomes brown and slightly ridged. The green stems are especially noticeable in winter when leaves are gone.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Small, pointed buds that hug close to the bright green stems. They're reddish-brown and alternate along the branches, never opposite each other.

habitat: Japanese kerria thrives in partially shaded areas with moist, well-drained soil, making it popular in woodland gardens and under trees. In New England, you'll mostly find it as a cultivated ornamental in residential landscapes, parks, and botanical gardens rather than growing wild. It tolerates various soil types but prefers spots protected from harsh winds and intense afternoon sun.

seasonality.spring: The main show begins with bright yellow flowers covering the arching branches, usually blooming from April through May. New leaves emerge bright green and fresh-looking.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and the shrub becomes a fountain of green foliage. Look for the distinctive arching growth habit and bright green stems.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn clear yellow before dropping, and the architectural form of the bare branches becomes visible. The green stems remain colorful.
seasonality.winter: The bright green young stems are the key identifying feature, creating colorful lines against snow. The graceful arching branch pattern is most visible now.

funFact: Japanese kerria is the only species in its entire genus worldwide - it's literally one of a kind! This makes it what botanists call a 'monotypic genus,' meaning this single species is so unique it gets a whole genus category all to itself.
confusionNotes: The bright yellow flowers might remind you of buttercups or marsh marigolds, but those are small wildflowers while kerria is a substantial shrub. The double-flowered variety 'Pleniflora' looks like yellow pom-poms and is sometimes confused with double daffodils, but it blooms on woody stems instead of from bulbs.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Japanese rose' and belonging to the rose family, kerria isn't a true rose at all - it lacks the thorns, compound leaves, and hip fruits that characterize real roses. In some parts of the southern U.S., it's romantically called 'Yellow Rose of Texas,' though it has no connection to that famous song.
compareHints: Since Japanese kerria is the only species in its genus, compare it to other rose family shrubs like spirea or ninebark. Unlike spirea's clusters of tiny flowers, kerria has larger single flowers that appear individually along the branches. Unlike ninebark's white or pink blooms, kerria's flowers are always bright golden-yellow and never fade to other colors.
